objections.title: Permit it and the option becomes a weapon against the weak — the elderly and disabled pressured, made to feel a burden, eased toward a door they never wanted; open it and you license atrocity, so it must stay shut for everyone.

objections.title: Grant the imposition-debt — that being forced into existence without consent creates a grievance owed compensation. The debtor is still the wrong party. You were imposed upon by your *parents*; they are the agents who acted. *Natalist society owes me a clean death* takes a debt incurred by procreators and bills it to the state, a third party that imposed nothing on you. Take it up with your parents. The state is a bystander you are dunning for someone else's liability — so it owes you nothing, and the claim-right to the means of dying, built on that debt, collapses with it.

objections.gloss: The argument slides from 'the option exists' to 'the institution asserts that disabled lives are worth less' — a step that holds only if availability-of-exit entails endorsement-of-exit-for-a-class…
objections.title: Legalize assisted dying and the law itself announces which lives society judges not worth sustaining — the disabled, the ill, the dependent. The option's mere availability is a message: that for people so situated, an exit is the intelligible, even fitting, response. Even if no one is pushed, the practice expresses that such lives are worth less, and that expressed judgment is a harm whatever any individual chooses.

objections.gloss: The argument conflates the profession's self-conception with the patient's right: even granting that some physicians regard ending life as outside their role, that fact about medicine's self-image…
objections.title: Assisted dying violates the integrity of medicine. The physician's role is to heal; 'first, do no harm' is the oath's spine. A doctor who helps a patient die has crossed from healer to killer, corrupts the profession's character, and erodes the trust that makes medicine possible — the patient's confidence that the person at the bedside is unconditionally on the side of their life.

objections.gloss: The objection vaults from 'this condition can impair some decisions' to 'this person can validly decide nothing about their own life' — an overgeneralization capacity assessment is built to refuse…
objections.title: You can't give valid consent to dying when you're mentally ill — the illness is making the choice, so honoring it isn't respecting autonomy, it's abandoning someone to their disorder.

objections.title: Good palliative and hospice care can control suffering to the very end — terminal sedation reaches even the cases nothing else does. So no one truly *needs* assisted death; they are driven to it by gaps in care. Fund palliation properly and the demand dissolves. Permitting death just lets us avoid fixing what is actually broken.

objections.gloss: The argument leaps from 'life has (sacred) value' to 'others may forcibly preserve this life against its bearer' — a license that only follows if the sanctity binds the agent without their consent…
objections.title: Life is sacred and inviolable — ending it is wrong whatever the person wants, and society may step in to honor that inviolability.

objections.title: Legalize assisted dying for the terminally suffering and the category will not hold. This is not hypothetical; it is the record. Canada's MAID regime expanded from reasonably-foreseeable death to Track 2 within a few years. Belgium and the Netherlands authorize euthanasia for psychiatric suffering and have moved into dementia. The gate, once cut, widens: chronic illness, disability, the psychiatric, the demented who can no longer consent, the merely tired of life, and at the far end the quietly coerced — the cost-pressured, the burden-fearing, the institutionally nudged. Each expansion is defended in the vocabulary minted for the last. The slope is already greased. The principle you license does not stay where you put it.

objections.gloss: The charge conflates a debt owed to others with a license to conscript the agent's continuation — but a debt grounds a claim against the agent, never the right to imprison them.
objections.title: Suicide is selfish — it dumps unbearable pain on the people left behind, who never consented to that grief.

objections.title: Suicide is a permanent solution to a temporary problem — whatever's driving it will pass, and then the irreversible choice is made on a feeling that would have lifted.
